<reason>Both sides were substantively strong, but Side A controlled the decisive clashes. A's symmetry-of-fallibility argument (CON's error standard would equally indict treatment refusal and palliative sedation) forced B into the act/omission distinction, which A persuasively characterized as selective. A's answer to the Canada drift—anchoring eligibility to diagnosis rather than suffering alone—was the cleanest resolution of B's best route, and while B's counter that courts dissolved a diagnosis line was sharp, it attacked only the entrenchment mechanism, not the diagnosis-anchor logic. Most decisively, B's concession in Rebuttal 2 ("I don't claim this reaches zero residual suffering") handed A a concrete residual-patient scenario that B never fully answered, and A's closing crystallized exactly that weighing. Both sides followed the Q/A format honestly and avoided fake precision; A's later speeches did more to narrow and resolve the dispute, while B's closing relied heavily on recapitulating the Canada argument.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange beginning at [A4.1]-[A4.4] and [B4.4]: A's "redundancy plus time" answer to the depression-screening pressure, plus the diagnosis-vs-suffering distinction defusing Canada, was met by B's clever claim that constitutional entrenchment is precisely what failed in Canada—but A's diagnosis-anchor point survived, and A then converted B's [B4.3] residual-suffering concession into the decisive weighing in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
